title: Efficiency Surveys
description: Efficiency surveys are excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(i): costs of studying or optimizing workflows or routine operations are not QREs.
summary: Efficiency surveys are expressly excluded from qualified research under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(D)(i) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(5), so U.S. businesses claiming the federal R&D tax credit cannot count costs of studying or optimizing workflows, management structures, or routine operations as QREs. Employee wage-allocation surveys differ, but uncorroborated survey percentages alone cannot substantiate a claim.

body.text: Efficiency surveys are expressly excluded from qualified research under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(D)(i) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(5), so U.S. businesses claiming the federal R&D tax credit cannot count costs of studying or optimizing workflows, management structures, or routine operations as QREs. Employee wage-allocation surveys differ, but uncorroborated survey percentages alone cannot substantiate a claim.

Under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41, "efficiency surveys" sit on a sharp legal fault line separating excluded business optimization from qualified technological research. By statute under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(D)(i) and Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(c)(5)(i), any substantive "efficiency survey" is expressly excluded from qualified research, disqualifying expenditures incurred to study or optimize internal workflows, management structures, or routine operations.
1. Statutory Baseline: IRC Section 41 and Qualified Research Expenses
1.1 Legislative Origin and Incremental Design

Congress enacted the federal research and experimentation tax credit in Section 221 of the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA, Pub. L. No. 97-34, 95 Stat. 172, 241–247), originally codified as former IRC Section 44F, to stimulate private-sector research spending after U.S. civilian R&D spending declined relative to Gross National Product during the 1970s. As documented in the 1981 legislative history, Congress concluded that a substantial tax credit for incremental research and experimental expenditures was needed to overcome the reluctance of ongoing companies to bear the significant staffing and supply costs and certain computer equipment charges required to initiate or expand research programs in a trade or business. ERTA initially scheduled the credit to expire on December 31, 1985, so Congress could evaluate whether the credit stimulated additional research spending and whether taxpayers and the IRS could accurately distinguish qualifying research expenditures from non-qualifying indirect overhead, administration, market research, quality control, or commercial production costs.

Subsequent legislation reshaped both the codification and substantive boundaries of the incentive. Sections 471(c) and 474(i) of the Tax Reform Act of 1984 (Pub. L. No. 98-369, 98 Stat. 494, 826, 831–832) redesignated former Section 44F as IRC Section 30. Section 231 of the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (Pub. L. No. 99-514, 100 Stat. 2085, 2173–2180) recodified the provision as IRC Section 41 within the general business credit framework of IRC Section 38(b)(4) and narrowed the definition of qualified research after Congress observed (H.R. Rep. No. 99-426, at 178) that taxpayers had applied the original Section 174-based definition too broadly to ordinary product development lacking technological innovation.

Under IRC Section 41(a) and 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-1(a), the research credit equals the sum of three components: (1) 20% of the excess (if any) of current-year QREs for the taxable year over the statutory base amount under Section 41(a)(1); (2) 20% of basic research payments determined under Section 41(e)(1)(A) and Section 41(a)(2); and (3) 20% of amounts paid or incurred by the taxpayer in carrying on any trade or business during the taxable year to an energy research consortium for energy research under Section 41(a)(3). Alternatively, taxpayers may elect the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under IRC Section 41(c)(5) and 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-9, which calculates the credit against prior-period QREs rather than fixed historical base-period gross receipts.

Because the Section 41 research credit is a component of the general business credit under IRC Section 38(a) and (b)(4), it operates generally as a limited nonrefundable credit against regular federal income tax liability (with unused credits carried from other years under Section 38(a)) and cannot offset Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) liability outside statutory exceptions for eligible small businesses (non-publicly traded corporations, partnerships, or sole proprietorships with average annual gross receipts for the preceding three-tax-year period not exceeding $50 million). Furthermore, under IRC Section 41(h), a "qualified small business"—defined under IRC Section 41(h)(3) as a business with less than $5 million in gross receipts for the current taxable year and no gross receipts for any taxable year preceding the 5-tax-year period ending with the current taxable year—may elect on Form 6765 (Section D) to apply a portion of its research credit as a payroll tax credit against federal employment taxes rather than against income tax liability.
1.2 Statutory Eligibility Criteria and Technical Clarifications

Under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A), qualified research requires research with respect to which expenditures may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174 (or, following the coordination amendment enacted by Pub. L. 119-21, domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174A). Under 26 C.F.R. Section 1.174-2(a)(1), this requires expenditures incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business that represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense.

Second, under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(i)–(ii) (comprising the "Technological Information Test" and the "Business Component Test"), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information which is "technological in nature," and the application of which is intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer. Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(a)(4) defines "technological in nature" verbatim: information is technological in nature if the process of experimentation used to discover such information "fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science". A taxpayer may employ existing technologies and rely on existing principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science to satisfy this requirement. Conversely, IRC Section 41(d)(4)(G) and Form 6765 instructions expressly exclude any research in the social sciences (including economics, business management, and behavioral sciences), arts, or humanities.

Third, under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and (d)(3)(A) (the "Process of Experimentation Test" and "Qualified Purpose" requirement), "substantially all" of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose—specifically relating to a new or improved "function," "performance," or "reliability or quality" of the business component. Under IRC Section 41(d)(3)(B) and 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), research is never treated as conducted for a qualified purpose if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. Under 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(a)(6), the "substantially all" requirement of Section 41(d)(1)(C) is satisfied "only if 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (and without regard to section 1.41-2(d)(2)), constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a purpose described in section 41(d)(3)". If the 80% threshold is met, the remaining 20% or less of research activities with respect to that business component also qualify so long as they satisfy Section 41(d)(1)(A) and are not otherwise excluded under Section 41(d)(4).

Fourth, under Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), a process of experimentation is defined as "a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities". Furthermore, 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) confirms verbatim that a process of experimentation involves identifying uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component, identifying one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty, and identifying and conducting a process of evaluating the alternatives "through, for example, modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial and error methodology". Notably, 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) emphasizes that mere uncertainty at the outset concerning a business component's appropriate design does not establish that all activities undertaken to achieve that component constitute a process of experimentation. Where an overall business component fails the 80% process-of-experimentation requirement or another prong of the four-part test, the "shrinking-back" rule of 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(b)(2) requires applying the tests to the most significant subset of elements of the product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention, continuing downward until either a subset of elements satisfies the requirements or the most basic element is reached and fails.
1.3 Statutory Scope of Qualified Research Expenses

Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A), in-house research expenses consist of three exhaustive categories: (1) any "wages" ( excluding any wages taken into account in determining the work opportunity credit) paid or incurred to an employee for "qualified services" performed by such employee; (2) any amount paid or incurred for "supplies" used in the conduct of qualified research (excluding land, depreciable property, indirect expenses, and general and administrative overhead under 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2); and (3) under regulations prescribed by the Secretary, any amount paid or incurred to another person for the right to use "computers" in the conduct of qualified research (which official Form 6765 instructions specify must be computer rental or lease costs for computers located off the taxpayer's premises where the taxpayer is not the operator or primary user).

Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3), the term "qualified services" encompasses three distinct categories of employee work. First, engaging in qualified research under Section 41(b)(2)(B)(i) and 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(c)(1) means "the actual conduct of qualified research (as in the case of a scientist conducting laboratory experiments)". Second, direct supervision of qualified research under Section 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(c)(2) means strictly "the immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research (as in the case of a research scientist who directly supervises laboratory experiments, but who may not actually perform experiments)," and explicitly excludes "supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that manager is a qualified research scientist"—a restriction known in tax practice and case law as the "one-up" rule. Third, direct support of qualified research under Section 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(c)(3) covers services in the direct support of either persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research or persons directly supervising them (such as a secretary typing reports describing laboratory results, a laboratory worker cleaning equipment used in qualified research, a clerk compiling research data, or a machinist machining a part of an experimental model), while explicitly excluding general administrative services (such as payroll personnel preparing salary checks of laboratory scientists, accountants accounting for research expenses, janitors performing general cleaning of a research laboratory, or corporate officers supervising financial or personnel matters, whether housed inside or outside the research department).

Under 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(e)(2)–(3), contract research expenses qualify only if paid pursuant to an agreement that: (i) is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, (ii) provides that the research be performed on behalf of the taxpayer (meaning the taxpayer has a right to the research results, even if not exclusive), and (iii) requires the taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful (any payment contingent on success is disqualified as a payment for a product or result rather than the performance of research). Furthermore, Congress established two higher statutory inclusion tiers under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(C) and (D): 75 percent for amounts paid or incurred to a "qualified research consortium" (a tax-exempt Section 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(6) scientific research organization that is not a private foundation) conducting research on behalf of the taxpayer and one or more unrelated taxpayers, and 100 percent for amounts paid to an eligible small business (500 or fewer employees), an institution of higher education (as defined in IRC Section 3304(f)), or a Federal laboratory (as defined in 15 U.S.C. Section 3703(6)) for qualified energy research.
2. Statutory Exclusion of Efficiency Surveys vs. Time-Allocation Surveys
2.1 Statutory Text and Regulatory Meaning of Excluded Efficiency Surveys

Even where an activity involves analysis, observation, or data gathering, it is statutorily disqualified from the research credit if it falls within the eight enumerated exclusions of IRC Section 41(d)(4)(A)–(H). Those eight statutory exclusions cover: (A) research after commercial production (when the component is developed to the point where it is ready for use or meets basic functional and economic requirements, including preproduction planning, tooling up for production, trial production runs, troubleshooting faults in production equipment or processes, accumulating production data, and debugging flaws); (B) adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need; (C) duplication (reproducing an existing business component in whole or in part from physical examination, plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information); (D) surveys, studies, management functions, market research, routine data collection, or quality control; (E) internal-use computer software developed primarily for general and administrative functions (financial management, human resources management, and support services), unless excepted or satisfying the high threshold of innovation test under 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(c)(6); (F) foreign research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States; (G) research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities; and (H) funded research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity where the taxpayer retains no substantial rights or does not bear financial risk.
The exact statutory text of 26 U.S.C. Section 41(d)(4)(D) reads:

(D) Surveys, studies, etc.—Any— (i) efficiency survey, (ii) activity relating to management function or technique, (iii) market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions), (iv) routine data collection, or (v) routine or ordinary testing or inspection for quality control.

Furthermore, efficiency surveys and management studies are excluded at the threshold Section 174 level as well: Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. Section 1.174-2(a)(3) (and (a)(6)) explicitly disallows Section 174 research and experimental expenditure treatment for the ordinary testing or inspection of materials or products for quality control, efficiency surveys, management studies, consumer surveys, advertising or promotions, the acquisition of another's patent, model, production or process, or research in connection with literary, historical, or similar projects.

Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(c)(5) (promulgated in Treasury Decision 8930, Jan. 3, 2001, and finalized in the December 2003 regulations) and official IRS Audit Techniques Guides (including the General Research Credit ATG, the Software Process of Experimentation Audit Guidelines, and the Aerospace Industry ATG) further define the scope of excluded surveys, studies, and management functions. Additionally, the IRS Aerospace Industry ATG confirms that workplace safety programs are generally evaluative in nature and therefore excluded as "surveys and studies" under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(D) (as contrasted with engineering safety features directly into a new or improved product design), and the IRS Pharmaceutical Industry Research Credit Audit Guidelines (revised April 30, 2004) verify verbatim that "Testing or inspection to determine whether particular units of materials or products conform to specified parameters is quality control testing".

Studies aimed at reducing labor overhead, measuring employee productivity, resequencing workflow queues, scheduling shifts, or rearranging workstations on an assembly line address business management efficiency rather than resolving uncertainty rooted in the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Crucially, however, the IRS Audit Techniques Guide emphasizes that "it is the activity which governs, not the intended end result. For example, the development of a new production process, which met all the tests for qualified research, would not be excluded simply because the activity was preceded by a management efficiency survey" (illustrated in 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 9). While the costs of conducting the management efficiency survey itself are 100% excluded under Section 41(d)(4)(D)(i)–(ii), subsequent engineering experimentation to design new automated machinery or a novel manufacturing process triggered by the survey's findings is evaluated independently on its own technical merits under Section 41(d)(1).

Under the governing hierarchy of federal tax authority—(1) Internal Revenue Code (26 U.S.C. Section 41), (2) Treasury Regulations (26 C.F.R. Sections 1.41-2 and 1.41-4), (3) binding federal appellate and Tax Court precedent, (4) IRS administrative guidance (Revenue Procedures, Internal Revenue Manual, Audit Techniques Guides), and (5) practitioner commentary—this semantic conflict resolves into two distinct legal rules. First, any substantive operational study, time-and-motion analysis, or management evaluation conducted to measure or improve operational workflow, labor efficiency, or organizational structure is a substantive "efficiency survey" or "activity relating to management function or technique" expressly disqualified from QRE eligibility by IRC Section 41(d)(4)(D)(i)–(ii) and 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(c)(5)(i)–(ii). Second, with respect to investigative wage-allocation questionnaires used during an R&D tax credit study, neither IRC Section 41 nor 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(d) mandates a single accounting method or daily timesheet system to allocate wages. In fact, the IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG) and the June 2005 Research Credit ATG (republished January 2008) expressly recognize that questionnaires, surveys, and interviews of technical and supervisory personnel may be employed during the execution of an R&D tax credit study, and instruct IRS examiners to request copies of any taxpayer surveys, responses, and instructions to verify how they were used in the credit computation. More importantly, under binding judicial precedent (Little Sandy Coal and Moore) and the IRS RCCATG, uncorroborated percentage estimates from employee surveys standing alone do not satisfy the substantiation burden of IRC Section 6001 and 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(d).

In the first scenario (Excluded Finance-Led Retrospective Time Allocation Survey), a company's Finance Department circulates a retrospective annual "Time Allocation Survey" at the request of the Chief Operating Officer (COO) to optimize assembly-line labor costs and simultaneously claim R&D tax credits, asking employees to estimate annual percentages across broad buckets such as "General Supervision," "Process Improvement," and "Non-Technical Project Management". Under verified law, this Finance survey fails on both substantive and evidentiary grounds: studying assembly-line labor costs to optimize operational efficiency is an excluded efficiency survey and management function under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(D)(i)–(ii) and 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(c)(5)(i)–(ii); "General Supervision" and "Non-Technical Project Management" fail the strict "one-up" immediate first-line supervision rule of 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(c)(2) and the exclusion of general administrative services under 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(c)(3); and broad labels like "Process Improvement" fail to segregate qualified experimentation under Section 41(d)(1)(C) from routine post-production troubleshooting or management-based workflow changes. In the second scenario (Compliant Contemporaneous Technical Tracking), an engineering department links daily or sprint-level project hours in an issue-tracking system to specific business components and documented technical uncertainties (such as resolving algorithmic latency or memory-allocation bottlenecks through comparative simulation and testing), which satisfies 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(d) by contemporaneously linking employee wages to specific business components and elements of a process of experimentation.

items: Step 1 — Proportional Qualified Wage Allocation (at 65%): $150,000 × (65 / 100) = $150,000 × 0.65 = $97,500 in Qualified Wages (QRE).
Step 2 — Proportional Excluded Wage Allocation (at 65%): $150,000 − $97,500 = $52,500 in Excluded Wages (verification sum: $97,500 + $52,500 = $150,000).

Step 3 — Application of the "Substantially All" Employee Wage Rule (at 80% or More): Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(d)(2), if "substantially all" of the services performed by an employee for the taxpayer during the taxable year consist of qualified services (engaging in qualified research, direct first-line supervision, or direct support), then the term "qualified services" means all (100%) of the services performed by that employee during the taxable year. Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(d)(2) specifies that this threshold is met "only if the wages allocated ... to services meeting the requirements of section 41(b)(2)(B)(i) or (ii) constitute at least 80 percent of the wages paid to or incurred by the taxpayer for the employee during the taxable year". Thus, at an 80% qualified allocation, strict proportional multiplication yields $150,000 × 0.80 = $120,000 (with $30,000 excluded), which 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(d)(2) elevates to 100% ($150,000 QRE and $0 excluded).

body.text: This conflates two legally independent 80% rules that Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(a)(6) explicitly instructs must be kept separate ("without regard to section 1.41-2(d)(2)"): the Activity / Business-Component "Substantially All" Rule under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(a)(6), which tests whether at least 80% of the research activities for a specific business component constitute elements of a process of experimentation (determining whether the project itself is qualified research); and the Employee-Service / Wage "Substantially All" Rule under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(d)(2), which tests whether at least 80% of an individual employee's annual wages are allocated to qualified services across qualified projects (determining whether the remaining 20% or less of that employee's annual wages may be grossed up to 100% QRE).
3. Substantiation Standards, Judicial Precedent, and Form 6765 Disclosures
3.1 Recordkeeping Burden Under 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(d)

Under IRC Section 6001 and Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. Section 1.6001-1(a), every taxpayer must "keep such permanent books of account or records ... as are sufficient to establish the amount of gross income, deductions, credits, or other matters required to be shown" on a tax return. Specifically for the research credit, Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(d) (approved under OMB Control No. 1545-1625) requires that a taxpayer claiming a credit under IRC Section 41 "must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit".

In Treasury Decision 8930 (2001) and current 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(d), the Treasury Department and IRS explicitly declined to mandate a uniform recordkeeping system or require researchers to record every experimental result in a prescribed format, recognizing that commercial R&D documentation varies across industries. Nevertheless, as the IRS RCCATG (citing Research, Inc. v. United States, 76 AFTR 2d 95-5688 (D. Minn. 1995)) and recent appellate decisions emphasize, general ledger payroll registers or W-2 wage summaries showing only how much compensation an employee received or how many total hours an employee worked are legally insufficient. Because general accounting systems do not align with IRC Section 41 definitions, taxpayers must produce competent, contemporaneous records (or corroborated project documentation) establishing a clear nexus between specific employees, specific business components, and specific qualified services. Furthermore, the IRS RCCATG instructs examiners that when taxpayers submit prepackaged "binder" studies, the taxpayer must direct the examiner to the specific underlying records substantiating the claim, and the IRS is under no obligation to accept uncorroborated estimates, extrapolations, or trending.

In reality, both the Tax Court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit denied 100% of the claimed research credits ("none of the expenses the subsidiary incurred in that development are qualified research expenses"). Taxpayer's shipbuilding subsidiary, Corn Island Shipyard, Inc. (CIS), claimed R&D credits across 11 vessel projects, represented at trial by two stipulated projects: Project 720 (the Apex 720 Tanker barge built for Apex Oil, Inc., claiming $2,505,491 in production wages, $17,504 in contract research, and $3,892,142 in supply costs) and Project 730 (the Detyens Dry Dock, a floating dry dock CIS had never previously designed, claiming $146,109 in production wages and $1,943,265 in supply costs, plus $609,276 in unassigned estimated engineering and management wages allocated via retrospective percentage estimates). The Tax Court and the Seventh Circuit rejected the claim in full under the 80% "substantially all" requirement of IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(a)(6). First, the courts held that the 80% test measures research activities, not the proportion of physical components that are "novel" or redesigned (rejecting the taxpayer's reliance on Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States). Second, the Tax Court held that production employees fabricating vessels (direct support) and physical supplies are not themselves "activities" engaged in a process of experimentation. Third, although the Seventh Circuit disagreed with aspects of the Tax Court's framing of pilot model fabrication, it affirmed the complete disallowance because CIS failed to document how much employee time was spent on a process of experimentation versus non-experimental fabrication and design. Writing for the Seventh Circuit, the court held that "shortcut estimates of experimentation-related activities will not suffice...[s]omething more, such as documentation of time spent on such activities, is necessary", and concluded that "Section 41(d) requires us to walk by sight, not by faith". Because CIS lacked project-by-project breakdowns of engineering and management activities, the courts also could not apply the shrinking-back rule under 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(b)(2).

Petitioner Gayla Moore was the sole shareholder of Nevco, Inc., an S corporation manufacturing sports-venue scoreboards and display equipment, which claimed flow-through Section 41 research credits for the 2014 and 2015 tax years (resulting in IRS income tax deficiency determinations of $68,263 for 2014 and $141,945 for 2015) across five products: Scoreboard Truss, Scorbitz, New Caney Ribbon Board, MPCX-2 wireless controller, and Slim Shot Clock. While the IRS conceded QRE treatment for Nevco's staff engineers and Director of Engineering Dave Paslay, Nevco also allocated 65% of the compensation (base salary of $85,092 in 2014 and $178,956 in 2015, plus bonuses) of its president and COO, Gary Robert—an engineer by training and a named inventor on the Scorbitz patent—based on oral testimony that Robert spent 50% to 65% of his time on "new product development". The Tax Court disallowed 100% of Robert's compensation across all three qualified-services prongs of IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B), and the Seventh Circuit affirmed in full. On direct conduct of research under Section 41(b)(2)(B)(i), even though Robert participated in product development meetings and helped define product requirements, "new product development" is a broad business category that includes non-qualified activities such as defining product specifications, market research, aesthetic design, customer feedback, and administrative planning; because Nevco kept no task-level records under 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(d) distinguishing the hours Robert spent on qualified technical experimentation from broader new product development, no portion of his time could be verified as direct research. On direct supervision under Section 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(c)(2), the Tax Court applied the "one-up" rule limiting direct supervision strictly to immediate first-line management of researchers; because the engineers reported directly to Director of Engineering Dave Paslay, and Paslay reported to Robert, Robert was two layers removed ("supervision of supervision") and disqualified from direct supervision as a matter of law. On direct support under Section 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(c)(3), Robert's executive oversight of personnel, inventory, and finance constituted excluded general administrative services rather than direct technical support. Writing for the Seventh Circuit on April 30, 2024, Judge Frank Easterbrook emphasized that while the substantive concept of experimentation includes simple trial-and-error "made famous by Thomas Edison," the evidentiary burden of proving and mathematically quantifying the fraction of time spent on qualified experimentation rests entirely on the taxpayer; without a verified numerator, the incremental credit equation cannot be solved.

In Cohan, the Second Circuit held that when a taxpayer proves entitlement to a tax deduction or benefit but cannot substantiate the exact dollar amount, a court may make a conservative estimate, "bearing heavily if it chooses upon the taxpayer whose inexactitude is of his own making". However, as documented in the IRS RCCATG and confirmed by the Seventh Circuit in Little Sandy Coal (62 F.4th at 308) and Moore, courts consistently refuse to invoke Cohan to rescue unsubstantiated R&D wage allocations. As the Seventh Circuit ruled in Little Sandy Coal, "Only after a taxpayer establishes that qualified research has occurred under Section 41(d) may we estimate, if needed, the amount of qualified research expenses under Section 41(b)". Where a taxpayer relies on generalized survey percentages without first proving that specific activities passed the four-part test and providing a credible evidentiary foundation to segregate qualified from non-qualified hours, Cohan provides no safe harbor. Even in rare cases where the Tax Court accepted manager interviews or surveys to allocate engineering wages—such as Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201—practitioner analysis notes that the taxpayer was a small company (~125 total employees and 40 engineers) whose Senior VP of Product Development had intimate personal knowledge of every project, backed the allocations with over 3,500 pages of trial testimony and 170,000 pages of contemporaneous exhibits, and still suffered a costly loss regarding the reasonableness of CEO compensation.
3.3 Updated Form 6765 Section G and Amended-Return Disclosure Rules
1. Form 6765 Section G (Business Component Information) Rules and Exceptions

Under the December 2025 Instructions for Form 6765, completing Section G is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 (unless filing an amended return) and becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025, subject to two statutory and administrative exceptions. Specifically, a filer is exempt from completing Section G if: (1) the filer is a qualified small business under IRC Section 41(h)(3) and checked the box to claim a reduced payroll tax credit; or (2) the filer's total QREs determined at the controlled group level on line 48 are equal to or less than $1.5 million, its average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years are equal to or less than $50 million (determined under IRC Section 448(c)(3) without regard to subparagraph 448(c)(3)(A)), and the filer is reporting a research credit on an original return.

Non-exempt filers must report by business component—in descending order by total QREs per business component, determined at the controlled group level (or at the separate-return member level for controlled group members filing separate returns)—a minimum of 80% of total QREs up to a maximum of 50 business components ("80%/Top 50"). Any remaining business components after identifying the 80%/Top 50 are reported on a single line by entering "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c) and entering their aggregate QREs in Columns 50 through 56, while leaving Columns 49(a), 49(b), 49(d), 49(e), and 49(f) blank. Paper filers with more than 15 business components attach additional sheets and sum them on the "Total from Attachments" line. Additionally, filers checking "Yes" on line 41 (utilizing the LB&I ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D Directive) make a single entry of "ASC 730 Directive" in Column 49(c) and report the Appendix B (Column A) totals in Columns 53–56; this entry does not count toward the 50-component cap, and if it equals at least 80% of line 48 total QREs, no additional business components need be listed.

For each reported business component, Section G requires granular data across Columns 49(a)–(e) and Columns 50–56. Column 49(a) captures the Employer Identification Number (EIN) of the entity conducting the research activities; Column 49(b) captures the Principal Business Activity (PBA) code from the top-level return; Column 49(c) captures the business component's name or unique alphanumeric identifier consistent with the taxpayer's books and records; Column 49(d) classifies the business component type exclusively as 1. Product, 2. Process, or 3. All Others (computer software, technique, formula, or invention); and Column 49(e) classifies software business components among A. IUS (Internal Use Software), B. DFS (Dual Function Software), C. Non-IUS, or D. Excepted from IUS treatment. Crucially, Columns 50–52 require disaggregating in-house wage QREs for each business component into Column 50 (wages of persons engaged in the actual conduct of qualified research), Column 51 (wages of persons engaged in immediate first-line direct supervision), and Column 52 (wages of persons engaged in direct support), followed by Column 53 (total qualified wages), Column 54 (qualified supplies), Column 55 (qualified computer rental/lease costs), and Column 56 (applicable contract research expenses).
2. Amended Return Refund Claims: The Five Items of Information and the June 18, 2024 Waiver (FAQ 21)
Originally, valid refund claims required providing "five items of information" at the time of filing:

items: Identify all the business components to which the Section 41 research credit claim relates for that year;
For each business component, identify all research activities performed;
Name the individuals who performed each research activity (or list titles/positions and headcount under FAQ 10 and FAQ 11);
Identify the information each individual sought to discover; and
Provide the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year.

body.text: Effective June 18, 2024 (FAQ 21), the IRS waived the requirement that taxpayers provide the two employee-specific detail items (Items 3 and 4: naming the individuals who performed each research activity and specifying the information each individual sought to discover) with the initial refund claim filing, reducing the initial upfront submission to the three remaining items (business components, research activities performed per component, and total wage/supply/contract QREs), though examiners may still request employee names and discovery narratives during substantive audit review. On Form 6765, Column 49(f) (describing the information sought to be discovered) is required only when claiming a refund or credit on an amended return for a Section 41 credit that was not reported on, or is increased from, the original return. Furthermore, the IRS twice extended the transition period allowing taxpayers 45 days to perfect a deficient Research Credit refund claim (notified via Letter 6426C or Letter 6428) through January 10, 2027, with a target IRS review timeframe of 6 months (noting under FAQ 15 that claims rejected as deficient or non-processible cannot be challenged before the IRS Independent Office of Appeals).
4. Compliant Wage Allocation Methodologies Replacing Excluded Surveys
4.1 Contemporaneous Technical Tracking and Corroborated Survey Frameworks

To overcome the evidentiary vulnerabilities highlighted in Little Sandy Coal and Moore and satisfy Form 6765 Section G, taxpayers should replace uncorroborated retrospective percentage questionnaires with project- and task-linked wage substantiation.

Where contemporaneous time-tracking or corroborated project records demonstrate that at least 80% of an employee's annual wages are allocated to qualified services under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B)(i)–(ii), 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(d)(2) permits including 100% of that employee's W-2 wages in QREs.

items: Educating Survey Participants on Statutory Exclusions: As documented in legal audit defense guidelines and the June 2005 IRS Research Credit ATG, survey respondents and interviewed department managers must be instructed objectively on what constitutes qualified research versus excluded activities under IRC Section 41(d)(4) (such as post-production debugging, adaptation to customer requirements, routine quality control, efficiency surveys, and higher-level management), and recording non-qualified time in the survey responses is essential proof that the instrument filters out excluded work.

Segregating Section G Service Categories and Enforcing the "One-Up" Rule: Survey instruments must never lump time into "New Product Development" or "General Supervision," but must instead separately capture (a) actual conduct of experimentation (Column 50), (b) immediate first-line supervision of researchers (Column 51, excluding managers who supervise other supervisors under 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(c)(2)), and (c) direct technical support (Column 52).

Mapping Allocations to Specific Business Components: Because IRC Section 41(d)(2)(A), LAFA 20212501F, and Form 6765 Section G require evaluating and reporting QREs separately by business component, survey allocations must assign employee time to specific business components (or documented component subsets under the 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(b)(2) shrink-back rule) rather than departmental cost centers alone.

Corroborating Survey Estimates With Contemporaneous Engineering Artifacts: To satisfy the Seventh Circuit's "walk by sight, not by faith" standard in Little Sandy Coal (62 F.4th at 308), periodic survey allocations must be cross-referenced against contemporaneous technical records—such as GitHub commit histories, Jira sprint tickets, CAD/simulation iterations, prototype test failure logs, patent applications, and architectural design reviews—that independently verify the existence of technical uncertainty and systematic evaluation of alternatives.

body.text: 4.2 Statistical Sampling Under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 and IRM 4.47.3

For large or multi-entity taxpayers where examining 100% of research projects, employees, or cost centers is prohibitively time-consuming and costly, the IRS permits probability-based statistical sampling governed by Revenue Procedure 2011-42 (2011-37 I.R.B. 318). Both the IRS RCCATG and Rev. Proc. 2011-42 draw a strict legal distinction between probability (statistical) samples—in which every sampling unit in the defined population has a known, non-zero chance of selection using either simple random sampling or stratified random sampling, enabling mathematically valid projection to the population—and judgment (non-statistical) samples, where selection relies on human judgment without known selection probabilities. Under the IRS RCCATG and Rev. Proc. 2011-42, taxpayers have no authority to project a judgment sample to compute the research credit on a return (unless mutually agreed in writing with the IRS examination team during an audit per the LB&I Field Directive), and unsubstantiated non-sampled units in a unilateral judgment sample are disallowed in full. Furthermore, IRS Legal Advice Issued by Field Attorneys (LAFA 20212501F, issued May 10, 2021) establishes that using statistical sampling under Rev. Proc. 2011-42—whether by the taxpayer to prepare a claim or by the IRS to audit a claim—does not alter, lessen, or change the object of analysis under IRC Section 41(d)(1): every sampled business component must still independently satisfy all four statutory tests, including the 80% "substantially all" process-of-experimentation requirement under 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-4(a)(6).

IRM 42(18) (specifically IRM 42(18)0 and IRM 42(18)3.4) is a superseded legacy manual citation from an older LMSB/LB&I Field Directive on sampling methodologies. Current IRS examination procedures are governed by IRM 4.47.3 (Statistical Sampling Auditing Techniques) (alongside IRM 4.47.1 and IRM 4.47.2 governing the Computer Audit Specialist (CAS) program under the LB&I Director of Field Operations South Central). Under IRM 4.47.3, IRS revenue agents submit a Specialist Referral System (SRS) request to a local CAS (mandatory for returns with activity codes of 221 and above), and a referral to a Statistical Sampling Coordinator (SSC) is strictly mandatory whenever: (a) an IRS examination team reviews and evaluates a taxpayer's statistical sample, (b) an IRS sample is designed with a projectable stratum containing fewer than 30 items, or (c) a Return Preparer penalty statistical sample is developed. CASs and SSCs test the validity of all taxpayer-proposed statistical samples using the mandatory LB&I Statistical Sampling Application.

Under Appendix A (Sampling Plan Standards), the taxpayer must prepare a written sampling plan prior to executing the sample that specifies all 10 mandatory items: (1) the plan's objective, including a description of the value being estimated and applicable tax year(s); (2) population definition and reconciliation to the tax return; (3) sampling frame definition; (4) sampling unit definition; (5) source of random numbers, starting point or seed, and selection method; (6) sample size determination and supporting factors; (7) method used to associate random numbers with the sampling frame; (8) steps taken to ensure frame serialization is carried out independently of drawing random numbers; (9) steps to be taken in evaluating each sampling unit; and (10) the appraisal method(s) to be used in appraising the sample. Under Appendix B (Sampling Documentation Standards), the taxpayer must retain the random seed, frame pairing records sufficient to retrace the process, a list of selected sampling units and evaluation results, supporting project documentation (notes, invoices, purchase orders, project descriptions), population projection and standard error calculations, a statement of any execution slips or blemishes, and associated adjustment computations. Under the 95% One-Sided Confidence Limit and 10% Relative Precision Rules, variable sampling estimates must generally use the least advantageous 95% one-sided confidence limit (the limit yielding the least tax benefit) unless the relative precision (sampling error at the 95% one-sided confidence limit divided by the point estimate, tested on a difference perspective when using difference, ratio, or regression estimators) is 10% or less, in which case the taxpayer may use the point estimate. If relative precision is greater than 10% and less than 15%, the allowable estimate is computed as a linear interpolation: Point Estimate − [(Relative Precision − 0.10) / 0.05] × (Point Estimate − Least Advantageous 95% One-Sided Confidence Limit). In attribute sampling plans, using the point estimate requires either achieving a relative precision of 10% or less on both the point estimate (estimated proportion p) and its complement (1 − p), or using a simple random sample size of at least 300 units (excluding dummy and null units). Statistical samples failing Section 4 of Rev. Proc. 2011-42 are rejected, limiting allowance strictly to examined units on an actual basis.

That claim directly contradicts the published December 2025 Instructions for Form 6765, which explicitly instruct: "If you used a statistical sampling methodology in accordance with Rev. Proc. 2011-42 to determine QREs, you must report the 80%/Top 50 business components as explained in the guidelines, irrespective of which business components were used for your statistical sample. You are required to maintain any records required by Regulations section 1.41-4(d) and section 6001". Under those published instructions, filers must also add the word "sample" to the end of the business component name or identifier in Column 49(c) for any listed component that was selected in the statistical sample, and report remaining components outside the 80%/Top 50 as "Aggregate Business Components". At the same time, as documented in KPMG's June 2026 Research Credit Audit Update, in March 2026 a senior IRS official publicly acknowledged that requiring statistical-sampling taxpayers to identify and report QREs by business component in Section G for non-sampled units contradicts the core purpose of statistical sampling—stating, "You shouldn't have to go outside your sample to identify things that you didn't look at because they weren't selected as part of the sample population"—and announced that the IRS intends to revise Form 6765 to correct this conflict. Until revised Form 6765 instructions are formally issued for 2026 returns, however, the published December 2025 Form 6765 Instructions remain the written administrative guidance on record.

Form 6765 Section G Effective Timeline & Exemptions

Statistical Sampling vs. Section G 80%/Top 50 Rule

Dec. 2025 Form 6765 Instructions state statistical sampling filers must still report 80%/Top 50 business components in Section G regardless of sample selection and append "sample" in Col. 49(c); in March 2026, the IRS acknowledged this drafting conflict and announced planned revisions.
Amended Return Refund Claim Disclosures

Form 6765 Col. 49(f) and refund validity disclosures apply to amended return credit claims; FAQ 21 (effective June 18, 2024) waived initial submission of the two employee-specific items (names and individual discovery narratives), leaving three required initial items; 45-day perfection window extended through Jan. 10, 2027.
Simplifies initial paper/fax or e-filed refund claim attachments while preserving the taxpayer's obligation to produce employee-level substantiation upon IRS examination.
IRS Examination & Specialist Review Authority

Governed by IRM 4.47.3 (Statistical Sampling Auditing Techniques), replacing superseded IRM 42(18). Computer Audit Specialists (CAS) and Statistical Sampling Coordinators (SSC) evaluate samples using the LB&I Statistical Sampling Application.

Referring a taxpayer statistical sample to an IRS Statistical Sampling Coordinator (SSC) is mandatory under IRM 4.47.3; workforce reductions in LB&I engineers alongside increased IRS AI risk modeling heighten the premium on clear, self-explanatory contemporaneous records.
